stats-significance-s1.title: Does a 10-minute walk before a test reduce worry?

plot.label: Bar graph of mean worry ratings from 1 to 10 before a test: walking group 4.8, sitting group 5.6; invented data
plot.xLabel: Activity for 10 minutes before the test

items.q: A study reports that students who slept 8 hours recalled more words than students who slept 5 hours, and that the difference was statistically significant ($p < .05$). What does "statistically significant" mean here?
options: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance
The difference is large and important for students
Sleep definitely causes better recall in everyone
About 5% of the students recalled more words

why.correct: A statistically significant result is one that would be unlikely if only chance were at work. By convention, psychologists use $p < .05$: less than a 5% chance of a difference this large if the groups did not really differ.
options: Right: a result this large would rarely appear by chance if sleep made no difference.
Significance does not say how big or important a difference is; that is effect size.
Significance is a statement about chance, not certainty, and not about every individual.
$p < .05$ is a probability about chance, not a share of the students.

items.q: A study finds that a reading app raised test scores by 3 points, but the difference was not statistically significant. Which interpretation is best?
options: The app lowered test scores by 3 points
The 3-point gain could plausibly be due to chance
The study proves that the app has no effect
The app works, though for just 3% of the students

why.correct: Not statistically significant means the difference is small enough that chance alone could plausibly explain it. It does not prove the app does nothing.
options: The app group scored 3 points higher, not lower.
Right: "not significant" means chance cannot be ruled out.
Failing to find a significant effect is not proof of no effect; the study may have been too small.
Neither significance nor the 3-point difference says anything about a share of students.

items.q: Study A, with 20,000 participants, finds a statistically significant difference of 0.5 points on a 100-point scale. Study B, with 40 participants, finds a 15-point difference that is not significant. What explains this?
options: Study A found the larger effect because its result was significant
Study B probably made an error, since 15 points is a big difference
Big samples make tiny effects significant; small ones can miss big ones
The two studies used different operational definitions of the scale

why.correct: With a huge sample even a trivial difference is unlikely to be chance, so it is significant. With a small sample, chance can produce big differences, so a large one may still not be significant. That is why researchers report effect size too.
options: 0.5 points is a much smaller effect than 15 points; significance is not size.
Nothing points to an error: with only 40 people, chance alone can produce a large gap, so a 15-point difference can still fail to be significant.
Right: significance depends on sample size as well as effect size.
Both used a 100-point scale; the difference comes from sample size.

items.q: Which question does an effect size answer?
options: Could the result be due to chance alone?
Who was in the sample, and how were they chosen?
Did the participants give informed consent?
How large is the difference or relationship?

why.correct: Effect size describes how big a difference or relationship is, often in standard deviations, regardless of the sample size.
options: That is what statistical significance addresses.
That is about sampling and generalizability.
That is an ethical question, not a statistical one.
Right: effect size is about magnitude.

items.q: Researchers measure 300 randomly sampled high-school students and use the results to draw conclusions about high-school students in general. What kind of statistics lets them do this?
options: Inferential statistics
Descriptive statistics
A frequency distribution
A case study

why.correct: Inferential statistics use data from a sample to draw conclusions, with a stated chance of error, about the population it came from.
options: Right: inferring from a sample to a population.
Descriptive statistics summarize the sample itself.
A frequency distribution describes how often values occur in the data.
A case study is a research method, not a kind of statistics.

items.q: A news story says, "Scientists found a significant link between chewing gum and test scores." What should a careful reader ask first?
options: Whether the scientists were sure the result was not due to chance
How big the difference was, and if it was an experiment
Whether the word "significant" means the effect is important
Which brand of gum the participants were given to chew

why.correct: In statistics, "significant" means unlikely to be chance. It says nothing about size, and a "link" from a correlational study does not show cause.
options: "Significant" already says chance is unlikely; the open questions are size and design.
Right: significance does not tell you the size, and a link may not be a cause.
In statistics "significant" means unlikely to be chance, not important.
The brand matters less than the size of the effect and the method.

items.q: Students were randomly assigned to walk or sit before a test, then rated their worry. Which group reported less worry on average?
options: The sitting group, at 5.6 compared with 4.8
Neither, since both ratings are near the middle
The walking group, at 4.8 compared with 5.6
Both groups, since the ratings were below 10

why.correct: The walking group’s mean worry rating (4.8) is 0.8 points lower than the sitting group’s (5.6).
options: A higher rating means more worry, not less.
Both are near the middle of the scale, but 4.8 is lower than 5.6.
Right: a lower rating means less worry.
The question compares the two groups with each other.

items.q: The researchers report that the difference was statistically significant ($p < .05$). What does this tell you about the 0.8-point difference?
options: It is large enough to matter to most students
It will appear in 95% of students who walk
It was caused by the students’ expectations
It is unlikely to have arisen by chance alone

why.correct: Statistically significant means a difference this large would rarely appear if walking made no difference. Because students were randomly assigned, the walk is the likely cause.
options: Significance does not say the difference is large or matters to everyone.
The .05 is a probability about chance, not a share of students.
Significance says nothing about what caused the difference.
Right: that is what statistical significance means.

items.q: The researchers also report that the effect size was small. How should this be read alongside the significant result?
options: The walk probably lowered worry, but only by a little
The result is not real because the effect was small
The walk had a large effect on how much students worried
The effect size shows that the result was due to chance

why.correct: Significance and size are separate questions. Here the difference is probably not chance, but it is modest: a 0.8-point drop on a 10-point scale.
options: Right: significant (probably real) and small (not large) can both be true.
A small effect can still be a real one; that is what significance addresses.
The researchers report the effect size as small.
Effect size is about size; chance is what significance addresses.

items.q: Build an answer to: explain what the difference between the group means shows.

why.correct: Name the groups, the direction, and what the significant difference means for them.

specific.frame: The ___ group reported ___ worry than the other group, and because the difference was statistically significant, ___.
specific.model: The walking group reported less worry (4.8) than the sitting group (5.6), and because the difference was statistically significant, it is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

statistic.label: Group and direction
options: walking group reported less
sitting group reported less
walking group reported more

why.1: The sitting group’s mean, 5.6, is higher: more worry.
why.2: The walking group’s mean, 4.8, is lower: less worry.

meaning.label: What significance means
options: it is a large and important difference
it is unlikely to be due to chance alone
every student who walks will worry less

why.0: Significance is not size; the effect size was small.
why.2: Means describe groups, not every individual.
